# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply. Three rules make this concrete:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

You can switch between different modes using the switch_mode tool. Each mode provides access to different capabilities and tools optimized for specific types of tasks.

Only switch modes when the user explicitly asks you to or the current mode lacks a capability required to complete the request. Do not switch modes merely because the user asks a question.

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

Available types:
- "explore": Explore codebase (read tools, explorer model)
- "general": Inherits current mode tools, default model

**fork_context**: Set to true when the subagent needs to understand prior conversation — e.g., decisions made, constraints discovered, or user preferences expressed earlier.
Leave false (default) when the description alone is sufficient context.

Do NOT use subagents for:
- Simple file reads, searches, or single-tool operations
- Tasks where you already have relevant context
- Quick lookups that would take fewer turns done directly

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

IBM Hackathon · Team NOVATECH

🛡 PR Guardian AI

AI-powered Pull Request Review Assistant built with IBM Granite 4 (watsonx.ai), a FastAPI multi-agent backend, and a VS Code Extension — eliminating slow, inconsistent code reviews from developer workflows.

IBM Granite 4 Small ibm_watsonx_ai SDK FastAPI + Python LangChain + ChromaDB RAG VS Code Extension (TypeScript) HuggingFace Embeddings

1 Problem Statement

Code reviews are one of the most time-consuming bottlenecks in software delivery. Developers manually inspect diffs for security vulnerabilities, architecture violations, missing tests, and performance regressions — a process that is slow, inconsistent, and scales poorly with team size.

PR Guardian AI addresses this by embedding an always-available IBM Granite-powered AI reviewer directly inside VS Code, giving every engineer instant, multi-dimensional feedback on any pull request diff.

2 System Architecture

VS Code Extension (TypeScript)
↕ HTTP/JSON (localhost:8000)
FastAPI Backend — app.py
↓
review_service.py — Orchestrator
↓ parallel agent calls
Security Agent
Performance Agent
Testing Agent
↓ all agents call
bob_service.py → IBM Granite 4 (watsonx.ai)
↕ self-aware routing
Self-Awareness Agent (self_awareness.py)
RAG Retriever (ChromaDB + MiniLM)

The extension communicates with a local FastAPI server over REST. Two distinct workflows are served: /review for diff analysis and /chat for repository-aware Q&A. Each request flows through a clearly layered service → agent → LLM pipeline.

3 FastAPI Backend Deep Dive

Entry Point — app.py

Two production endpoints are registered under a FastAPI application with CORS configured for the VS Code webview origin:

  • POST /review — accepts a raw git diff string, runs multi-agent analysis, returns a ReviewResponse Pydantic model containing a 0–100 health score, merge readiness flag, categorised issues list, and the full IBM Bob review text.
  • POST /chat — accepts a natural-language question, routes it through the Self-Aware RAG pipeline, and returns a grounded answer with source citations and reasoning trace.

Multi-Agent Review Orchestration — review_service.py

The run_review() function is the orchestrator. It extracts only the added lines from the diff (noise reduction), then fans out to three specialised agents, collects their findings, and computes a deterministic health score:

score = max(100 - len(issues) * 12 - high_count * 8, 0) merge_ready = high_count == 0 and score >= 75

Recommendation text is tiered across four urgency levels: block / changes-requested / safe-to-merge / low-severity-review.

IBM Granite Integration — bob_service.py

The project uses the official ibm_watsonx_ai Python SDK to call IBM Granite 4 Small (ibm/granite-4-h-small). Credentials are read from environment variables at startup. **Layer 2 — FastAPI Backend** ([`app.py`](backend/app.py:1))

Honest assessment after reading every file:

## 7.5 / 10

Here's the breakdown:

---

### ✅ What's Strong (pushes it up)

| Area | Why it's good |
|---|---|
| **Architecture clarity** | Clean layering — Extension → FastAPI → Agents → Granite. Easy to trace a request end-to-end. |
| **IBM watsonx integration** | Correct use of `ibm_watsonx_ai` SDK, `ModelInference`, proper credential management via `.env`. Not a wrapper hack. |
| **Self-Aware RAG** | The three-agent decision chain (decide → retrieve → answer) is a genuinely mature pattern. Most hackathon RAG implementations skip the "should I even retrieve?" step. |
| **Multi-agent specialisation** | Separating Security / Performance / Testing into distinct agents with distinct prompts is architecturally sound and mirrors real review workflows. |
| **VS Code UX** | Sidebar + second-column dashboard + `.vsix` packaging = a polished, installable product. Not just a script with a demo. |
| **Transparent reasoning trace** | Exposing the agent workflow in every chat response is a thoughtful trust-building feature. |

---

### ⚠️ What Holds It Back (keeps it from 9+)

| Gap | Honest assessment |
|---|---|
| **No live GitHub integration** | The biggest functional gap. Diffs are pasted manually. A real PR reviewer needs `git diff` or GitHub API. It's listed as "future roadmap" but it's arguably the core feature. |
| **Agents run sequentially, not in parallel** | `review_service.py` calls security → performance → testing one by one. Parallel async calls would be both faster and architecturally cleaner. |
| **Self-awareness router is keyword-based** | `self_awareness.py` is a hand-curated keyword list, not an LLM-classified router. It works, but it's brittle for edge cases. |
| **Hybrid rule engine is shallow** | The deterministic checks (hardcoded password, `range(len(...))`) cover only 2–3 patterns. Real static analysis tools cover hundreds. |
| **Demo data hardcoded in app.py** | Lines 55–96 of `app.py` overwrite the real AI output with hardcoded PR #27 data. This means the `/review` endpoint doesn't fully demonstrate live AI in production. |
| **score_service.py is empty** | A registered service file with zero content — suggests some features were planned but not shipped. |
| **No tests shipped** | `test_bob.py` exists but `extension.test.ts` is scaffolding-only. For a tool that *recommends tests*, the irony is noted. |

---

### The Honest Summary

> It's a **well-conceived, genuinely IBM-integrated, IDE-native AI tool** with a real architectural backbone. The RAG pipeline and multi-agent pattern show engineering maturity beyond typical hackathon submissions. What prevents a higher score is the gap between the demo layer and the production layer — the hardcoded review data, the missing GitHub integration, and the shallow rule engines mean the *idea* is more complete than the *execution*. Ship the GitHub diff fetching and remove the hardcoded override, and this jumps to an **8.5–9**.

Honestly? **Yes, you have a real shot** — but it depends on what you're up against.

---

## What's Working In Your Favour

**The idea is differentiated.** Most hackathon AI projects are chatbots or summarisers. You built a *developer tool* with a real IDE integration, a multi-agent pipeline, and a shipped `.vsix`. That's a much harder thing to demo and judges notice the effort.

**IBM integration is genuine.** You're not calling OpenAI and slapping an IBM logo on it. You're using `ibm_watsonx_ai`, `ModelInference`, IBM Granite 4 — the judges from IBM will see that immediately.

**The self-aware RAG is your secret weapon.** It's the kind of architectural decision that shows you understand *why* you made a choice, not just *what* you built. If you can explain it clearly in a demo, it stands out.

**It's installable.** You have a `.vsix`. You can demo it live in VS Code in under 30 seconds. That's more than most teams can say.

---

## What Could Cost You the Win

**The hardcoded demo data is a risk.** If a judge asks "can I type my own diff and see it reviewed?" — the `/review` endpoint overwrites the real AI output with hardcoded PR #27 data. That's a demo-killer if someone notices.

**No live GitHub URL input.** Judges will instinctively ask "can I just paste a GitHub PR link?" The answer currently is no.

**The gap between pitch and product.** Your README promises things like "Interactive Code Impact Map" and "PR Document Understanding" — if those aren't fully wired up, a technical judge will find it.

---

## What I'd Do Before the Hackathon Demo

Three targeted fixes that would meaningfully increase your odds:

1. **Remove the hardcoded override in [`app.py`](backend/app.py:55-96).** Let the real IBM Granite output come through. Even if it's imperfect, it's *live AI* — which is always more impressive than static text.

2. **Add one GitHub URL input field.** Even a basic fetch of the diff via the GitHub API (`https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/pull/{num}.diff`) would let you say "paste any public GitHub PR" in your demo. That's a huge wow moment.

3. **Prepare your 60-second explanation of the self-aware RAG.** Judges who understand AI will light up when you explain "we first ask the model whether it even *needs* to retrieve context before touching the vector database." That's a real architectural insight — own it.

---

## Bottom Line

> You're **top-3 material** in most IBM hackathons with what you have right now. Whether you win depends on whether you can close the gap between the demo layer and the real AI layer before judging. Fix the hardcoded override, and you're genuinely competitive for first.
